children.text: A highland valley about 1,300 m above sea level, just north of Baguio, and the Philippines' main strawberry-growing area. You can pick strawberries yourself at the Benguet State University farm, then see the March Strawberry Festival and the vegetable trading post, all in half a day.
La Trinidad is the capital of Benguet province, a highland basin town right next to Baguio City, only about
6 km
to the north. Its fields lie on a valley floor about 1,300 m above sea level, and in January the daytime high is around
and the night low around

, so it stays cool. It supplies most of the Philippines' strawberries and cut flowers such as roses, which earned it the nicknames "Strawberry Fields of the Philippines" and "Rose Capital," and its berries are shipped to markets across the country.
The heart of the strawberry farm that travelers visit is the farm owned by Benguet State University (BSU) in Barangay Betag. BSU opened in

as the La Trinidad Farm School and has carried out agricultural research on this land ever since. According to published sources, the farm covers about 79 ha, around 660 farming households lease plots of 500–1,000 m² each, and the annual harvest in
was about 1,775 tons. It is easier to think of it not as a single farm but as a "strawberry village" where neighboring fields and greenhouses line both sides of the road.
The numbers show how popular it is. According to the Benguet tourism office, about 540,000 people visited this farm in the first half of
, the most of any site in the province, and La Trinidad as a whole counted about 700,000 visitors in
. The strawberry season runs from
November
to
June

, and thanks to greenhouse growing you can see some strawberries even outside the season. The town government has declared strawberries its One Town, One Product (OTOP) item, and the whole town really does revolve around them.
Many travelers confuse this place with Baguio, but administratively it is not Baguio City but La Trinidad, Benguet. In

the town government drew up a tourism code urging that the name "La Trinidad" be promoted clearly. It adds only half a day to a Baguio itinerary, and it suits families with children, travelers who enjoy picking and eating their own fruit and browsing produce markets, and those stopping by on the way north to Sagada or Atok along the Halsema Highway.

You walk between the rows of a farm plot and pick ripe red strawberries yourself. The usual system is to weigh and pay for them right after picking, and in peak season self-picked strawberries are said to cost about
/kg. That is more than strawberries sold at the stalls outside the farm, but the fun of choosing the ripest berries is worth the price.

Along the dirt road running from the entrance to the farm, stalls selling strawberry jam, strawberry wine, souvenirs, and clothes stand shoulder to shoulder. The big strawberry sculpture and the "Welcome" sign are popular photo spots. On weekend afternoons the crowds slow you down, so take your time.

blocks.title: Viewing the valley from a deck

children.text: Some farms have bamboo viewing decks where you can look out over the whole valley above the strawberry rows. Rows covered in white plastic and hillside villages in the distance fit into one frame. The light is best in the late afternoon, when the sun is low and the clouds clear.
Around "Strawberry Lane" at the entrance road, stalls sell strawberry sorbetes (street ice cream), strawberry taho, strawberry cupcakes, and similar treats. A cone of sorbetes usually costs around
, which makes it easy to eat while walking. We suggest picking a stall you like and trying just one item at a time.
The La Trinidad Strawberry Festival, held every
March
, is the town's biggest event. In
the town baked the world's largest strawberry shortcake (about 9,622 kg) and set a Guinness World Record, and in
it served about 12,000 cupcakes at
each from
March 3–24
. The schedule and events change every year, so check announcements before you go.

The La Trinidad Trading Post is a wholesale market where highland vegetables come together. Benguet is known as the "Salad Bowl," said to supply about 80% of the highland vegetables sold in Metro Manila, and the sight of cabbages, carrots, potatoes, and lettuce piled up like hills is a highlight. The busiest trading happens at early hours, so if you sleep in you may see only a quiet market.

The BSU campus near the farm has a university museum, an orchidarium, and a suspension bridge over the Balili River. As an agricultural university, it has trial plots all around, so you can see vegetable fields as well as strawberries. Opening hours and entry conditions depend on the school, so check on site.
Leave central Baguio by jeepney or taxi. Mornings are best, before the roads get congested
Arrive at the BSU strawberry farm entrance and browse the market stalls while choosing a farm plot
Strawberry picking. Even one basket makes a nice souvenir and gives you plenty of photos
Take valley photos from the viewing deck and have strawberry sorbetes and taho as snacks
Choose strawberry jam and strawberry wine at the souvenir stalls
Have lunch, then return to Baguio by jeepney or taxi

Whether flower farms are open depends on the season and each farm's circumstances. Check on a Facebook page or at a local information desk before visiting, and if it rains in the afternoon, it is better to drop the flower fields and focus on the museum and the market.
Direct buses to Baguio, such as Victory Liner, run from Manila (Monumento, Cubao, Pasay) almost every hour. The trip takes about
4–7 hours
, and fares are listed from about
for a regular air-conditioned bus to about
for a non-stop deluxe bus. From the Baguio bus terminal, transfer to a jeepney or taxi to La Trinidad.
The most common plan is to stay a night in Baguio and visit the strawberry farm the next day. A dawn bus from Manila arrives late in the afternoon, so a day trip is hard.
Fly from Manila to Clark International Airport (CRK), then take a bus or chartered van from Clark to Baguio. Clark to Baguio is said to take about
3–4 hours
depending on road conditions, so leave some slack in your schedule.
From Baguio to La Trinidad, see "Getting around from Baguio" below.
The usual route is to drive down NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX toward La Union and then climb a mountain road (such as Kennon Road) to Baguio, and Manila to La Trinidad is about
254 km
. The mountain roads often have rockfalls and fog in the rainy season, so travel in daytime.
Parking near the farm entrance is hard to find on weekends. Arrive early and use a nearby public or private parking lot.
A jeepney from central Baguio toward La Trinidad takes about
20–40 minutes
. The distance is only about
6 km
, but traffic is heavy at rush hour and on weekends. The fare is said to be about
, so have small change ready when you get off.
A taxi or Grab takes about
10–15 minutes
when the road is clear and costs roughly
. Get out at the farm entrance and walk in, and since it is hard to catch a ride back, it is easier to negotiate a round-trip charter.
The paths inside the farm are dirt and get muddy when it rains. Getting around is usually on foot or by small tricycle.

The Halsema Highway toward Atok and Sagada starts in Baguio and runs north through La Trinidad. If you are coming back from Sagada or Atok, it is easy to plan a stop in La Trinidad to buy strawberries on the way.
Landslides are frequent on the Halsema Highway in the rainy season, so check road conditions before you set out.
La Trinidad sits a little lower than Baguio, so it is slightly milder, but it is still a cool highland. The strawberry season of
November–May
is mostly dry, so the field paths are dry and the skies clear, which makes walking pleasant. Strawberries start to bear fruit around
November
and continue until
June
, but from
March
the days warm up and you walk the rows under a hot sun.
In the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers and typhoons are frequent, and
August
is the wettest month. The fields turn to mud and fruit in the plastic greenhouses spoils easily, so don't expect to pick strawberries then. The busiest times are the
March
Strawberry Festival, Holy Week, and the year-end holidays, so book lodging and transport in advance if you go then.

La Trinidad itself has homestays and small lodgings, but Baguio is far better for choice, restaurants, and transport. Most travelers stay in Baguio and visit La Trinidad for a day or half a day. Central Baguio has many guesthouses and mid-range hotels at about
per night. Rooms fill quickly during the Strawberry Festival and the year-end holidays, so book ahead.

The food here is, above all, strawberries. Eating freshly picked berries as they are is the basic pleasure, and strawberry taho (a warm tofu pudding topped with strawberry syrup), strawberry sorbetes, and strawberry cupcakes are the signature snacks. Locals turn strawberries into jam, dried fruit, tarts, cookies, wine, vinegar, and even soap, so browsing for souvenirs is fun too. A salad or soup made with Benguet vegetables and a cup of highland coffee make a meal.
Early morning is best for strawberries. The fruit is fresh in the morning light and there are fewer people, while heat and crowds grow once it turns to midday.
Before picking, ask the farm staff about the price, how you pay (whether by weight), and whether you may eat as you pick. The rules differ from farm to farm.
Bring sneakers or waterproof shoes, a hat, and sunscreen. The ground between the rows is slippery after rain and the sun is strong at midday.
Keep the strawberries you take home in their basket in a cool place, and since they bruise easily, eat them the same day if possible.
Most entrance stalls and street vendors take cash only. Bring plenty of small bills.
Spend one morning of your
Baguio
trip in La Trinidad, then return in the afternoon to Burnham Park or the downtown night market for an efficient route.
On weekends and holidays the entrance road gets crowded after
9 AM
. Choose a weekday if you can.
Farm opening hours, entry conditions, and the Strawberry Festival schedule can change, so check the town's tourism announcements or local information just before you go.

Check the weight unit and the price before you pick. In peak season self-picked strawberries cost more than those at the stalls, and some farms charge separately for eating as you pick. If you start picking without knowing how you will be charged, you may pay more than you expected.
On weekends, in Holy Week, and during the March Strawberry Festival, the entrance road and parking lot are very crowded. Watch out for pickpockets and keep valuables in a bag you wear in front.
Some fields may use pesticides or fertilizer, so it is safer to wash picked strawberries in clean water before eating them.
In the rainy season the field paths turn to mud and landslides can occur on mountain roads such as the Halsema Highway. Postpone your trip on days with a strong rain forecast.
Do not touch seedlings, stems, or other crops in the farm without permission. This is the farmers' livelihood.
It gets chilly after sunset in the highlands. Bring a light jacket.
